documents.name: berth-plan.md
documents.body:
# Plan a berth

You book a berth before the vessel arrives. Open the berth plan and pick a
slot. The plan shows which quays are free for the window you need.

If two vessels want the same slot, the plan flags the clash. Move one of them
or shorten the stay. You can save a draft and come back to it.

Confirm the booking when the times are settled. Harbourlight tells the terminal
and the agent.

documents.name: manifest.md
documents.body:
# Read a manifest

Every call has one manifest. It lists what is on board, who owns it, and where
it goes next.

Open the manifest from the call view. Filter by consignee to find one shipment,
or by hazard class to find what needs special handling.

A manifest changes while the vessel is at sea. Harbourlight keeps each version,
so you can see what the crew declared and when.

documents.name: arrivals.md
documents.body:
# Track arrivals

The arrivals board shows every vessel due in the next seven days. It updates
when the vessel reports a new position.

Sort by estimated arrival to see what lands first. Pin a vessel to keep it at
the top while you work.

If an estimate moves by more than two hours, Harbourlight marks the row and
tells anyone who pinned it.

documents.name: roles.md
documents.body:
# Set up roles

Give each person the access their job needs and no more.

A planner books berths and edits plans. A clerk reads manifests and files
customs paperwork. A supervisor does both and can undo either.

Change a role from the team page. The change takes effect on the next sign-in.

documents.name: customs.md
documents.body:
# File with customs

File before the vessel berths. Late filings hold the cargo on the quay.

Harbourlight builds the filing from the manifest. Check the consignee details
and the hazard codes, then submit.

Customs answers within the hour. If the filing is rejected, the reason appears
on the call view and the clerk who filed it is told.

documents.name: alerts.md
documents.body:
# Choose your alerts

You decide what Harbourlight tells you about.

Turn on arrival changes to hear when an estimate moves. Turn on clash alerts to
hear when two vessels want one berth. Turn on customs alerts to hear when a
filing is answered.

Alerts go to email by default. Add a phone number if you want them by text.

documents.name: overview-marketing.md
documents.body:
# Harbourlight Overview

Harbourlight is a revolutionary port logistics platform that allows operators to
utilize a single pane of glass across every terminal touchpoint. Organizations
can leverage our best-in-class scheduling engine to deliver seamless berth
allocation at scale.

documents.name: release-notes.md
documents.body:
# Release Notes

This release introduces game-changing improvements to the manifest viewer,
allowing users to utilize filters that were previously unavailable.

Performance has been improved and the experience is now seamless.

documents.name: onboarding-email.md
documents.body:
# Welcome

We are delighted to welcome you to Harbourlight, the best-in-class solution
trusted by leading operators worldwide.

Our team will reach out shortly to help you leverage the full breadth of the
platform's revolutionary capabilities.

documents.name: help-passive.md
documents.body:
# Berth Allocation

A berth may be allocated by a planner once the vessel's estimated arrival has
been confirmed by the agent. It should be noted that allocations which have
been submitted cannot subsequently be amended by users other than those to whom
supervisory permissions have been granted, and any such amendment will be
recorded in the audit trail that is maintained by the platform for the purpose
of subsequent review.

documents.name: faq-thirdperson.md
documents.body:
# Frequently Asked Questions

How does the operator amend a filing?

The operator navigates to the call view, where the operator selects the filing
in question. The operator then submits an amendment, which the system routes to
customs on the operator's behalf.

Harbourlight utilizes a globally distributed infrastructure to deliver a

Should degradation occur, remediation is initiated automatically and affected
parties are notified in due course.

steer.guide:
# Voice Guide: Harbourlight

Plain, direct voice for a port logistics tool

## Tone
- Personality: plain, direct, calm
- Formality: neutral
- Emotion: neutral
- Humor: none
- Guidelines: Address the reader as you. State what to do next. No superlatives, no hedging.

## Style Rules
- Use active voice
- Sentence length: short
- Point of view: second
- Contractions: sometimes
- Prohibited patterns:
  - passive construction (severity: major)
  - hedged filler (severity: minor)

## Vocabulary
### Forbidden Terms
- ~~utilize~~
- ~~leverage~~
- ~~best-in-class~~
- ~~seamless~~
- ~~revolutionary~~
- ~~game-changing~~

docs.task: Write a short help page, about 120 words, explaining how a port operator files cargo paperwork with customs before a vessel berths.
docs.bare:
# Filing Cargo Paperwork Before Vessel Berthing

Port operators must submit cargo documentation to customs no later than 24 hours before a vessel's scheduled arrival. Begin by preparing the cargo manifest, listing all containers, bill of lading numbers, consignee details, and HS classification codes for each shipment.

Submit the manifest through the customs electronic filing portal, attaching supporting documents including the bill of lading, certificate of origin, and any required import permits. Verify that hazardous materials declarations are included where applicable.

Once submitted, customs will issue a filing reference number. Monitor the portal for clearance status or requests for additional information. Vessels will not be granted berthing clearance until the customs authority confirms that all cargo paperwork has been accepted and processed.
docs.steered:
# Filing Cargo Paperwork Before Berthing

You must submit cargo paperwork to customs before the vessel berths.

## Steps

1. Confirm the cargo manifest matches the bill of lading. Check quantities, weights, and consignee details.
2. Submit the manifest through the customs portal at least 24 hours before arrival. For vessels arriving within 24 hours of departure from the last port, submit as early as possible.
3. Attach supporting documents: certificate of origin, dangerous goods declaration (if applicable), and the vessel's arrival notice.
4. Wait for customs clearance confirmation. Do not schedule berthing until you receive it.
5. If customs flags a discrepancy, correct the manifest and resubmit. Berthing cannot proceed until the flag clears.

## Notes

Late submissions delay berthing. File as soon as the manifest is final. Keep a copy of the clearance confirmation for the vessel's records.

docs.task: Write a short help page, about 120 words, explaining how a port operator resolves two vessels booked into the same berth at the same time.
docs.bare:
# Resolving a Berth Double-Booking

When two vessels are booked into the same berth for overlapping windows, the system flags the conflict on the berth schedule and neither booking is auto-cancelled — you must resolve it manually.

**Steps:**

1. Open the **Berth Schedule** and locate the conflicting bookings (shown in red).
2. Check each vessel's ETA/ETD, draft, and priority class (e.g. scheduled liner service vs. ad hoc call).
3. Decide which vessel keeps the slot. Consider tidal windows, cargo urgency, and contractual priority.
4. Reassign the other vessel to an alternative berth, or adjust its time window if the same berth is available later.
5. Update the booking — the system will notify both vessel agents automatically.
6. Add a note to the booking record explaining the resolution, for audit purposes.

If no alternative berth or slot is available, escalate to the Harbour Master for a priority ruling.
docs.steered:
# Resolving a Berth Double-Booking

Two vessels booked into the same berth at the same time create a conflict. Follow these steps to resolve it.

1. Open the berth schedule and confirm the overlap. Check both booking windows against the berth's actual availability.
2. Check each vessel's priority tier, arrival time, and cargo type. Use these to decide which vessel keeps the berth.
3. Contact the operator of the vessel you plan to move. Confirm the change before you touch the schedule.
4. Reassign the lower-priority vessel to an open berth, or shift its window earlier or later.
5. Update the schedule and notify both vessel operators, the pilot, and the tug crew.
6. Log the conflict and its resolution in the incident record.

If no alternate berth is available, escalate to the duty manager before you make a decision.

docs.task: Write a short release note, about 120 words, announcing that the arrivals board now updates when a vessel reports a new position.
docs.bare:
Vessel Positions Now Update the Arrivals Board in Real Time

The arrivals board now refreshes automatically whenever a vessel reports a new position. Previously, estimated arrival times only updated on a fixed schedule, which meant the board could lag behind a vessel's actual progress. Now, as soon as a new position report comes in, the corresponding arrival estimate is recalculated and reflected on the board immediately.

This means port operators, agents, and other stakeholders relying on the arrivals board always see the most current, accurate arrival estimates, without needing to manually refresh or cross-check against other sources. Delays, route changes, and speed adjustments are all picked up as they happen, reducing the gap between what a vessel is actually doing and what the board shows.

No configuration changes are required to take advantage of this update.
docs.steered:
Arrivals board now updates automatically when a vessel reports a new position.

Previously, the board refreshed on a fixed schedule, so a position report could sit unreflected for several minutes. Now, each report updates the vessel's row as soon as it arrives. You'll see revised ETAs and status changes without reloading the page.

This applies to every vessel with an active voyage on the board. If a vessel goes quiet, its last known position stays visible with a timestamp, so you can tell how current the data is.

No setup is required. If you have the arrivals board open, changes appear in place. If you notice a gap between a report and the board, refresh the page and let your port contact know.

docs.task: Write a short help page, about 120 words, explaining how an administrator gives a new colleague the right level of access.
docs.bare:
# Granting Access to a New Colleague

As an administrator, you control what a new colleague can see and do by assigning them a role when you add them to your organization.

**To grant access:**

1. Go to **Settings → Members** and select **Invite member**.
2. Enter their email address and choose a role:
   - **Viewer** — can view content but not make changes.
   - **Editor** — can create and edit content within assigned projects.
   - **Admin** — full access, including managing members and billing.
3. Optionally, restrict access to specific projects or workspaces rather than the entire organization.
4. Send the invitation. Your colleague will receive an email to set up their account.

You can change a member's role or remove their access at any time from the Members page. Start with the least access needed, then expand it as their responsibilities grow.
docs.steered:
# Setting Access for a New Colleague

When you add a new colleague, choose the role that matches their job, not their seniority. Start with the lowest role that lets them do their work. You can raise it later.

**Roles**
- **Viewer** — reads content, runs no changes.
- **Editor** — creates and edits content in assigned projects.
- **Admin** — manages users, roles, and settings.

**Steps**
1. Open **Settings > Users**.
2. Click **Invite Colleague** and enter their email.
3. Assign a role and, if needed, limit it to specific projects.
4. Send the invite.

Your colleague gets an email with a link to set up their account. You can change their role or remove access at any time from the same page. Every change you make here is logged.

Your Harbourlight account is set up. You can now log in and start tracking vessel movements, berth schedules, and cargo status across your terminal.

**Filing Delays — Resolved**

Between approximately [start time] and [end time] UTC, filings submitted through our platform experienced processing delays of up to two hours. During this window, filings were accepted and queued normally but were not confirmed or transmitted to their destination as quickly as usual.

The underlying issue has been identified and resolved. All delayed filings have since been processed, and the queue has fully caught up to real-time processing as of [end time] UTC.

No filings were lost during this incident, and no further action is required from users. If you submitted a filing during the affected window and have not received confirmation, please check your filing history or contact support.

We apologize for the inconvenience and are reviewing safeguards to prevent recurrence.
